title: Are splay trees dynamically optimal?
formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For example, imagine alternating long phases that repeatedly access two different small clusters of keys. A static layout must compromise between the clusters; an adaptive tree can reorganize between phases. The challenge is to pay for reorganization only when it is justified, even when an adversary changes the pattern. This is an illustrative example, not a new lower bound.

The 2026 analysis compares splaying directly to a moving optimal tree. Its remaining multiplicative factor still grows with n. Removing that factor would establish a universal constant-competitive guarantee, not merely another locality-sensitive upper bound.

why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
definitions: The key set is fixed: this card concerns searches, not insertion and deletion. Offline means that the comparator knows the complete request sequence. The root-BST model is shown equivalent, within constant factors, to the standard BST model in Appendix B of the 2026 paper.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.
Tango trees give an online BST with an $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying.
The preprint proves $O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

status_note: Constant competitiveness remains open in the July 2026 source; its nearly optimal bound is a preprint result.
review_scope: Read the 2026 statement, model, theorem, and conclusion; checked the earlier Tango guarantee and teaching source. No independent proof verification.
review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.
answer_criterion: Prove one universal constant competitive bound with the stated additive initialization term, or prove that the ratio cost_splay/(OPT+n) is unbounded over initial trees and access sequences.

importance.reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
